How does Kubernetes FQDN resolve to an I: When a Service is created, Kubernetes registers a DNS record for it in the cluster's internal DNS (CoreDNS) following the pattern `<service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`. When a Pod queries that name, its DNS resolution (configured via `/etc/resolv.conf`, pointing at CoreDNS) forwards the query to CoreDNS, which looks up the Service's registered ClusterIP and returns it - same-namespace calls can use the short name alone (`service-name`) thanks to the search domains also configured in the Pod's resolv.conf, while cross-namespace calls need the fuller form.
What is the role of CoreDNS in Kubernete: CoreDNS is the cluster's internal DNS server, providing name resolution for Services and Pods. It watches the Kubernetes API server (via the standard watch mechanism, same as any controller) to stay updated on Service/Endpoint changes, maintaining an in-memory mapping of names to ClusterIPs - so yes, it does communicate with the API server, but only to stay informed of Service state, not to serve every individual DNS query through it (queries are answered directly by CoreDNS from its own cached view).
Is CoreDNS a bridge between etcd and the: No - CoreDNS never talks to etcd directly (nothing does except the API server itself). CoreDNS is a DNS server that watches the API server (like any other controller/client) to learn about Services and Endpoints, then answers DNS queries from Pods based on that information - its role is purely name resolution within the cluster, not any kind of intermediary or bridge in the API server/etcd relationship.
What is RBAC in Kubernetes? Why do we us: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) governs who can perform which actions on which resources within Kubernetes, used to enforce least-privilege access rather than everyone having full cluster access. A `Role` defines permissions scoped to a single namespace; a `ClusterRole` defines permissions that can apply cluster-wide (or be reused across namespaces). A `RoleBinding` grants a Role's permissions to specific users/groups/service accounts within that namespace; a `ClusterRoleBinding` grants a ClusterRole's permissions cluster-wide - the Role/ClusterRole defines *what* is allowed, and the Binding defines *who* gets it.
Suppose an application goes down in a Ku: The kubelet on the node running that Pod continuously executes the configured liveness/readiness probes against the container - if a probe fails, kubelet updates the Pod's status and, for a failed liveness probe, restarts the container itself. Kubelet reports this status change back to the API server (which persists it to etcd), which is how the control plane 'knows' - it's kubelet actively detecting and reporting, not the control plane polling out to check on applications directly.
Which component detects that a pod or ap: Kubelet is the component that actually detects unhealthy Pods - it runs the configured liveness/readiness probes on each container locally on its node, and acts on the result directly (restarting a container that fails liveness, marking a Pod NotReady if readiness fails) before even reporting the status upward - kubelet is the active enforcer, not just a passive reporter.
Is kubelet a worker node component or a: Kubelet is a worker node component - it runs on every node (including, in some cluster topologies, control plane nodes if they also run workloads) and is responsible for managing the Pods scheduled to that specific node, distinct from control plane components (API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd) which are typically dedicated to and fully managed on the control plane in managed Kubernetes like GKE.
How does kubelet communicate with the co: Kubelet communicates exclusively with the API server (never directly with etcd or other control plane components) - it registers the node, reports node and Pod status, and watches the API server for Pods assigned to it that it needs to run. The API server is the single gatekeeper and source of truth for all cluster state, validating and persisting every read/write (to etcd) that any component, including kubelet, makes.
Explain the Liveness Probe. When is it u: A liveness probe periodically checks whether a container is still functioning correctly (via an HTTP call, a TCP check, or an exec command) - used to detect a container that's technically running but stuck/deadlocked and unable to recover on its own. If it fails (repeatedly, per the configured failure threshold), kubelet kills and restarts the container, since the assumption is that a restart is the only way to recover from whatever state it's stuck in.
Explain the Readiness Probe. How is it d: A readiness probe checks whether a container is currently able to serve traffic - if it fails, the Pod is removed from the Service's endpoints (no traffic routed to it) without being restarted, letting an app signal 'temporarily busy/still starting up' gracefully. The key difference from liveness: readiness failure changes traffic routing only, while liveness failure triggers an actual container restart - conflating the two (e.g. using only a liveness probe for a temporarily-busy condition) causes unnecessary restarts of a perfectly healthy, just-busy container.
If an application gets stuck or becomes: No - `kubectl` is just a client tool for humans to talk to the API server; Kubernetes itself never runs kubectl internally. The restart is triggered directly by kubelet on the node, which detects the liveness probe failure and instructs the container runtime (via the CRI - Container Runtime Interface) to stop and restart the container - this happens entirely at the node level without going back through the API server for the restart action itself.
How does kubelet restart a failed contai: Yes - kubelet communicates directly with the container runtime (containerd, CRI-O) via the Container Runtime Interface (CRI), a standardized gRPC API. When a liveness probe fails or a container exits unexpectedly, kubelet instructs the runtime via CRI to stop and start a new container instance, then reports the updated status back to the API server - the actual restart mechanics happen locally on the node without needing to go back to the control plane first.
What is the complete flow when an applic: The application container crashes -> kubelet (running on that node) detects it either via the container runtime reporting the exit or a failed liveness probe -> kubelet restarts the container directly via the CRI (for a same-Pod restart) and updates the Pod's status -> kubelet reports this status to the API server -> the API server persists the updated status to etcd -> if the failure requires a different kind of remediation (e.g. the Pod itself needs to be recreated, as with a Deployment's ReplicaSet controller noticing a Pod is gone), the relevant controller in the controller manager, which watches the API server for state changes, detects the discrepancy between desired and actual replica count and creates a new Pod to reconcile it.
What do you mean by content correlation: Correlation in an observability context means linking related signals - a metric spike, the corresponding logs from the same time window, and a distributed trace showing the exact request path - together by a shared identifier (commonly a trace ID or request ID) so an engineer investigating an incident can pivot directly from 'this metric looks wrong' to 'here are the exact logs and trace for one of the affected requests' instead of manually cross-referencing timestamps across disconnected tools.
